meta.name: Google Cloud Professional Cloud Architect
meta.notes: [bulk-tag pass: added `gcp-pca` tag to 61 questions] | 2026-07-30 hardening pass: full pack rewrite — fixed truncated options (`,.` / `;.` fragments) across 25+ questions, removed leaked explanation fragments, added per-distractor 'why wrong' analysis to every explanation, removed stale 'option A/B/C/D' references (options are not lettered), balanced correct-index distribution to 15/15/15/15 across the 60 single-answer questions, swapped weak or implausible distractors for realistic near-miss GCP services, ensured correct answer is not systematically the longest option.

questions.question: A company has 10 GCP projects across 4 teams. The security team requires all outbound internet traffic to pass through a single centralized proxy. Which architecture satisfies this requirement while minimizing operational overhead?
options: Give each project its own VPC and full-mesh VPC peer them to a proxy project, adding proxy routes in every peer.
Configure a Cloud NAT gateway in each project sharing one external IP range so egress converges on the proxy.
Create a Shared VPC in a host project, attach all service projects to it, and add a default route pointing to a proxy instance group.
Provision a Cloud Interconnect back to the on-premises perimeter proxy and force every project's egress over it.
questions.explanation: Shared VPC centralizes networking in a host project: service projects consume its subnets, firewall rules and routes, so a single default 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing at the proxy transparently steers every project's egress. Full-mesh VPC peering does not propagate custom routes transitively, so a project two hops away from the proxy VPC would never see the route. Cloud NAT gateways only translate source addresses to the internet — they do not send traffic through an inspection proxy. Cloud Interconnect backhauls traffic to on-prem gear but keeps the network topology fragmented across projects and adds an unnecessary hybrid dependency for a purely GCP-native requirement.

questions.question: A global fintech needs a database for 50,000 transactions per second across five continents with strong external consistency, ACID transactions, and p99 latency under 10 ms. Which service is the best fit?
options: Bigtable configured with multi-cluster routing and application-side conflict resolution.
Cloud Spanner deployed in the nam-eur-asia1 multi-region configuration.
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with cross-region read replicas in each continent.
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL with asynchronous cross-region replication.
questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner is the only fully managed relational service on GCP that combines horizontal write scaling, ACID transactions and externally consistent reads across regions; the nam-eur-asia1 configuration spreads replicas across three continents while preserving global consistency. Bigtable is a wide-column store: it is eventually consistent when using multi-cluster routing and does not offer relational ACID semantics. Cloud SQL scales reads through replicas but writes remain confined to a single primary, so it cannot sustain 50k global writes/second. AlloyDB replicates asynchronously across regions, so remote replicas can lag — that violates the strong-consistency requirement.

questions.question: A media company serves video globally and must terminate TLS as close to viewers as possible while routing to the nearest healthy backend behind a single IP. Which architecture delivers that with the least latency?
options: Deploy Traffic Director with Envoy sidecars in each region to control routing between clients and backends.
Place regional External HTTPS load balancers in every major region and steer users with Cloud DNS geolocation policies.
Front the origin with Cloud CDN configured for origin failover across multiple Cloud Storage buckets.
Configure a Global External HTTPS Load Balancer with a single anycast IP, backed by regional backend services.
questions.explanation: The Global External HTTPS Load Balancer advertises one anycast IP from every Google edge; TLS is terminated at the nearest PoP and traffic then rides Google's private backbone to the closest healthy backend, minimizing both handshake and transit latency. Traffic Director is an xDS control plane for service meshes — it programs proxies but is not itself a global HTTPS frontend for internet clients. Regional load balancers with DNS geo-steering still terminate TLS in the destination region, so a client hits a distant PoP for the handshake and gets no anycast failover. Cloud CDN caches responses but requires a load balancer front end to accept and terminate TLS in the first place.

questions.question: An IoT platform ingests events from one million devices. Analytics, alerting and archival services must each process every message independently, without coupling the device producers to any single consumer. Which pattern fits?
options: Have each device call a central Cloud Function that fans out synchronous requests to every downstream service.
Use Cloud Tasks with a queue per downstream service, having devices push tasks into each queue directly.
Publish to a single Pub/Sub topic and create a separate subscription for each downstream service.
Land raw events in a Cloud Storage bucket and let each consumer poll the bucket for new files.
questions.explanation: Pub/Sub's fan-out model gives every subscription an independent copy of the topic's messages and its own cursor and backlog, so analytics falling behind can never starve the alerting subscription — precisely the decoupling the scenario needs. A synchronous Cloud Function fan-out couples producer latency to the slowest consumer and multiplies device retries whenever any consumer hiccups. Cloud Tasks is designed for HTTP-style task execution, not durable pub/sub fan-out, and would force devices to know about every consumer. Polling a Cloud Storage bucket adds minute-scale ingestion latency, per-request listing cost and no per-consumer cursor to guarantee each service sees every event exactly once.

questions.question: A mobile game needs a database that auto-scales with users, pushes real-time updates to mobile clients, and handles offline access with conflict resolution. Which GCP database fits best?
options: Cloud SQL for MySQL fronted by the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy so mobile clients can reach it directly.
Firestore in Datastore mode with a Memorystore cache layer to serve reads.
Firestore in Native mode using real-time listeners and the client SDK's offline persistence.
Bigtable accessed through a custom mobile SDK with a client-side cache.
questions.explanation: Firestore Native mode is designed for mobile and web: real-time listeners push changes over WebSockets, and the client SDK caches data locally so writes queue when offline and reconcile via last-write-wins conflict resolution when connectivity returns. Cloud SQL has no push-to-client model, needs long-lived TCP connections that mobile networks cannot reliably hold, and is not intended for direct client access. Datastore mode has no real-time listener API — the mobile SDK is available only for Native mode — and a Memorystore front does nothing for offline writes. Bigtable has no mobile SDK, no listener protocol and no offline sync layer, so all three of the mobile requirements would have to be built from scratch.

questions.question: A genomics company stores 100 TB/month of raw sequencing data. Files must be immediately accessible for 30 days, retrievable within an hour for one year, and archived cheaply thereafter. Which lifecycle policy minimizes cost?
options: Standard for 30 days, then Nearline, then Coldline after 365 days for long-term archival.
Skip Standard entirely by starting on Nearline from day 1, then move to Archive after 365 days.
Standard for 30 days, then Nearline, then Archive after 395 days (30 + 365) for long-term archival.
Standard for 30 days, then Coldline directly, then Archive after 365 days.
questions.explanation: Nearline (30-day minimum, ms-scale access) matches the 'retrievable within an hour for one year' band cheaply, and moving to Archive at 395 days (30 + 365) hits the long-term-cold cost floor. Coldline has a 90-day minimum storage duration, so paying its early-delete fees during the 30-to-395 day window costs more than Nearline. Starting on Nearline from day 1 violates the immediate-access requirement in the first 30 days and forfeits the free Standard reads that period would enjoy. Skipping Nearline and moving straight from Standard to Coldline at day 30 pays the higher Coldline rate for a full year when Nearline would have been cheaper for that same access pattern.

questions.question: A logistics Pub/Sub topic delivers shipment events. The warehouse-management system (WMS) and the customer-notification service must each process every event independently, and the WMS is currently backlogged. How should the pipeline be designed?
options: Share one pull subscription between the two services and filter messages on the client side.
Create a separate pull subscription for each service on the same topic so each maintains its own backlog.
Use Pub/Sub Lite with a fixed partition assignment for each service.
Insert a Dataflow pipeline that reads one subscription and writes to two Cloud Storage buckets, one per service.
questions.explanation: In Pub/Sub, each subscription is an independent copy of the topic's stream with its own cursor and backlog, so a slow WMS subscription cannot delay or drop deliveries to the notification-service subscription. A single shared subscription load-balances messages between competing consumers, meaning any given event is processed by only one of the two services, not both. Pub/Sub Lite trades global scalability and management overhead for a partition model built for high-throughput cost efficiency, and does not solve the independent-backlog requirement any better than plain Pub/Sub subscriptions. Fanning through Dataflow to Cloud Storage adds batch latency and cost for what a native pull subscription already provides.

questions.question: A data-science team runs daily batch ML feature-engineering jobs on 200 GB Cloud Storage datasets. Each job takes about two hours and runs once per day. Which compute approach minimizes cost?
options: Keep a persistent Dataproc cluster sized for peak load with autoscaling enabled.
Use a Dataproc workflow template that creates an ephemeral cluster, runs the job and deletes it.
Rewrite the pipeline as BigQuery ML SQL to avoid managing any cluster at all.
Run a persistent Dataflow streaming pipeline that continuously processes files as they arrive.
questions.explanation: An ephemeral Dataproc cluster driven by a workflow template is created just before the job, runs the two-hour job, then is deleted — so you pay for two hours per day instead of twenty-four. A persistent cluster sits idle 22 hours a day and keeps billing for the master and worker VMs. BigQuery ML can be a good landing spot for some feature work, but rewriting a 200 GB Spark/PySpark pipeline in SQL is a substantial migration and is not a cost-minimising move by itself. A persistent streaming Dataflow pipeline is designed for continuous ingestion; for a once-a-day batch job it burns worker capacity 24×7 that it does not need.

questions.question: A company runs containerized workloads across GCP, AWS and on-premises data centres. They want one control plane for policies, service mesh and configuration across all environments. What is the recommended solution?
options: Register clusters everywhere as GKE Enterprise (Anthos) fleets with Config Sync and Anthos Service Mesh.
Push identical Kubernetes manifests to every environment from a central Jenkins pipeline.
Wrap each environment with Cloud Run so infrastructure differences are hidden behind one runtime.
Write a Terraform module and a custom Kubernetes operator that keep configurations in sync across providers.
questions.explanation: GKE Enterprise (formerly Anthos) is Google's multi-cloud control plane: clusters on GCP, AWS, Azure and on-prem register to a shared fleet, Config Sync applies GitOps configuration and policies to all of them, and Anthos Service Mesh provides consistent mTLS, traffic policy and observability across the mesh. A central Jenkins pipeline can apply YAML, but has no runtime enforcement, no drift reconciliation and no service mesh — every guarantee has to be rebuilt by hand. Cloud Run does not exist as a portable runtime on AWS or on-prem; it also cannot enforce Kubernetes-level policy across arbitrary clusters. Terraform plus a bespoke operator is exactly the roll-your-own solution that GKE Enterprise's fleet features exist to replace.

questions.question: A telecom stores billions of network-performance metrics collected every minute from 10 million devices over five years. Every query is a time-range scan for a specific device. Which storage design is optimal?
options: Cloud SQL for MySQL with a composite index on (device_id, timestamp) and monthly range partitioning.
Cloud Spanner with a parent-child interleaved table keyed on device_id for locality on per-device scans.
BigQuery with a time-partitioned table clustered on device_id for cheap analytical scans across all devices.
Bigtable keyed on {device_id}#{reverse_timestamp} so device rows cluster and recent data sorts first.
questions.explanation: Bigtable is built for wide, high-throughput time-series storage; the {device_id}#{reverse_timestamp} row key groups every device's samples together while placing recent samples first, so a per-device range scan reads one contiguous block. Cloud SQL cannot horizontally scale to billions of rows across five years and its per-instance write ceiling would bottleneck ingest. Cloud Spanner solves for strong consistency and global scale but is significantly more expensive per GB than Bigtable for opaque time-series and is over-engineered for a pattern that never needs cross-row transactions. BigQuery excels at analytical scans, not at single-device point-in-time lookups — its minimum query latency and per-scan cost make it a poor fit for interactive time-range reads.

questions.question: A startup deploys a Python web API with sporadic traffic — hours of idle followed by hundreds of RPS during bursts. They want zero idle cost and no pre-warmed capacity. Which option fits best?
options: Deploy the API on Cloud Run with min-instances set to 1 to avoid cold-start latency at all times.
Deploy on Cloud Functions 2nd gen with a scheduled warm-up trigger during business hours.
Run the API on App Engine Standard, which scales to zero and bills only for active request time.
Use GKE Autopilot with KEDA scaling the deployment down to zero pods between bursts.
questions.explanation: App Engine Standard scales to zero when idle and bills in 100 ms increments for actual request handling, so an idle service costs nothing and burst traffic gets on-demand instances — exactly the request. Cloud Run with min-instances=1 keeps one billed instance running at all times, which contradicts the 'zero idle cost' constraint. A scheduled Cloud Functions warm-up keeps instances alive on a fixed timetable regardless of traffic and re-introduces the cost the question wants to avoid. GKE Autopilot with KEDA can scale pods to zero, but you still pay for the control plane and the reconciled minimum cluster overhead — heavier and more expensive than App Engine Standard for a sporadic Python API.

questions.question: A SaaS application on Cloud Spanner shows write hotspots because its primary key is a monotonically increasing order_id. Throughput is capped by a single split. Which schema change resolves the hotspot?
options: Add a secondary index on order_id so reads and writes distribute across additional splits.
Rewrite the primary key as a bit-reversed or hash-prefixed order_id so writes spread across splits.
Adopt a composite primary key of (customer_id, order_id) so writes shard across the customer dimension.
Switch the primary key to an application-generated random UUIDv4 to remove sequential order entirely.
questions.explanation: Spanner splits ranges by key order, so a monotonically increasing key always writes at the rightmost split. Bit-reversing the sequence or prepending a short hash produces uniformly distributed keys, letting writes spread across splits — this is Google's canonical Spanner anti-hotspot pattern. A secondary index on the same monotonically increasing column just moves the hotspot to the index. A composite (customer_id, order_id) key only helps if customer IDs are themselves diverse and there is no dominant customer — many workloads still hotspot on the top customer. UUIDv4 removes the hotspot but discards any ordering guarantees, and its full 128-bit random values make range scans and secondary indexes larger than necessary, so bit-reversed sequential UUIDs are preferred.

questions.question: A retailer has a 50 TB BigQuery table with ten years of sales data. Analysts always query one specific region across a one-month date range. Which optimization delivers the best cost and performance?
options: Split the dataset across regions with BigQuery Omni so each region has its own smaller table.
Partition by region_id and cluster by transaction_date because region is the primary filter.
Create a materialized view grouped by region_id and month for the most common aggregates.
Partition by transaction_date and cluster by region_id so both partition pruning and block-level scan reduction apply.
questions.explanation: Date partitioning prunes to the queried month, discarding ten-plus years of data before scanning, and clustering by region_id lets BigQuery skip blocks within the surviving partitions where the region does not match — the two mechanisms compose. Partitioning by region_id first produces one partition per region (small, uneven, and BigQuery caps you at 4,000 partitions in any case), which loses the temporal pruning that dominates the query cost here. A materialized view accelerates aggregate queries but does not help ad-hoc drill-downs that select raw rows, and it still needs the base table to be partitioned/clustered for the refresh to be cheap. BigQuery Omni is for querying data that lives in AWS or Azure — moving in-region data across it does not reduce scans.

questions.question: A financial firm moves 100 GB/day of trading data from on-premises to GCP. They need guaranteed bandwidth, low latency, and traffic must never traverse the public internet. Which connectivity option fits?
options: Dedicated Interconnect: a 10 Gbps physical circuit into Google's network at a colocation facility.
Direct Peering into a Google edge peering location — a private path that does not run over the internet.
HA VPN with two Cloud VPN tunnels and BGP, backed by a 99.99% SLA.
Partner Interconnect through a service provider for cheaper managed private connectivity.
questions.explanation: Dedicated Interconnect is a physical private circuit between the on-prem network and Google's edge at a supported colocation site; traffic runs over Google's private network end-to-end and carries an SLA when deployed redundantly, satisfying the guaranteed-bandwidth and no-public-internet requirements. Direct Peering exchanges public routes at a peering point — it is not intended for private VPC connectivity and does not carry a VPC-level SLA. HA VPN builds IPsec tunnels over the public internet, which directly violates the 'never traverses the public internet' constraint even though it does have a 99.99% SLA. Partner Interconnect is also private, but the extra provider hop typically means lower per-link bandwidth ceilings and a shared SLA path — for a firm that specified 'guaranteed bandwidth', Dedicated Interconnect is the stronger match.

questions.question: An infrastructure team uses Terraform across three environments. They need to prevent concurrent state modifications, share state between engineers, and audit every state change. Which native GCP backend achieves this?
options: The GCS backend pointed at a dedicated versioned bucket with object-level locking.
The local backend combined with an NFS-mounted state file and file locking.
A Cloud SQL row storing the JSON state with row-level locks for concurrent access.
Terraform Cloud's remote backend for built-in locking and audit trails.
questions.explanation: The Terraform GCS backend keeps state in a Cloud Storage bucket, uses GCS's native object locking to block concurrent writes, and — with object versioning enabled — retains every prior state generation for auditing. That combination is the GCP-native answer to all three requirements. A local state file on NFS has no reliable cross-host locking and no audit trail; it is discouraged for team use. Cloud SQL as a Terraform backend is not a first-class option and would require a bespoke shim to marshal and lock state. Terraform Cloud is a third-party HashiCorp SaaS service — it works, but it is explicitly not a native GCP backend, which is what the question asked for.

questions.question: An ML team runs GPU training on GKE three times a week for about four hours per run. They want zero GPU cost between runs. Which GKE configuration achieves that?
options: Create a GPU node pool with minimum-nodes=0 plus taints and tolerations so only training pods land on it.
Deploy the GPUs on Spot preemptible node pools and accept restarts mid-run.
Turn on Cluster Autoscaler with scale-down-enabled=true against the GPU node pool.
Use GKE Autopilot and let it provision GPU nodes on-demand for the training workloads.
questions.explanation: Setting the GPU node pool's minimum to zero and gating it with taints/tolerations is the canonical zero-idle pattern: pods without the toleration never schedule there, and once training pods finish the autoscaler removes the last GPU node so the bill drops to nothing. Spot GPU pools do reduce the price per hour but do not deliver zero cost between runs and expose training jobs to preemption without a checkpoint plan. Cluster Autoscaler alone will scale the pool down, but without a minimum-nodes=0 configuration the pool retains its floor, and without taints ordinary pods can still keep a GPU node warm. GKE Autopilot's GPU support is incomplete — several GPU types and configurations still require Standard node pools — so relying on Autopilot alone can silently prevent the workload from scheduling.

questions.question: A team wants Infrastructure-as-Code for GCP using only Google-supported native services — no third-party tooling. Which option satisfies that?
options: Cloud Functions triggered by Cloud Storage events that create resources imperatively.
Config Connector: a Kubernetes operator that reconciles GCP resources from Kubernetes manifests.
Cloud Composer DAGs orchestrating gcloud calls from Airflow operators.
Cloud Deployment Manager (legacy) using YAML/Jinja2 or Python templates.
questions.explanation: Config Connector is Google's supported, actively developed native IaC option: install the operator into a GKE cluster and every GCP resource is expressed as a Kubernetes CRD that Config Connector continuously reconciles. Cloud Functions can create resources, but that is imperative scripting with no desired-state reconciliation, no drift correction, and no dependency graph — it is not IaC in the meaningful sense. Cloud Composer running gcloud is likewise imperative orchestration, and Airflow is an Apache project, not native GCP. Cloud Deployment Manager is native but has been placed in maintenance mode with no new features and a formal deprecation path, so Google now points customers to Config Connector or Terraform.

questions.question: A web app on Managed Instance Groups sees unpredictable spikes. The app takes 90 seconds to initialize. Which MIG configuration ensures new instances are ready before traffic hits them?
options: Drive autoscaling from Pub/Sub queue depth combined with a 90-second bootstrap script that signals readiness at the end.
Enable predictive autoscaling in OPTIMIZE_AVAILABILITY mode so instances are pre-provisioned before every expected spike.
Set a 90-second initialization period on the autoscaling policy and pair it with a backend-service warm-up on the load balancer.
Set the autoscaling cooldown period to 90 seconds and drive scaling from CPU utilization as the primary signal.
questions.explanation: The autoscaler's initialization period tells the MIG not to count freshly created VMs against the target metric until the app has had time to become healthy, and the backend service's warm-up period tells the load balancer to withhold full traffic during that same window. Together they prevent traffic from reaching an instance that is still starting. Predictive autoscaling helps when traffic is periodic and predictable, but the scenario explicitly says the spikes are unpredictable — prediction based on the past does not apply. Pub/Sub queue depth is irrelevant to a synchronous web app; and a bootstrap script by itself does not stop the load balancer from routing traffic during those 90 seconds. Cooldown just throttles further scaling decisions — it does not delay traffic to the new instance.

questions.question: A startup wants Kubernetes without managing node pools, worker nodes or cluster upgrades, and wants to pay only for pod requests. Which GKE option fits?
options: Cloud Run on GKE for containerized workloads with no need for direct Kubernetes API access.
GKE Standard with node auto-upgrade and node auto-repair enabled.
GKE Autopilot, which manages nodes for you and bills per pod request.
GKE Standard with an Autopilot-mode node pool attached to the cluster.
questions.explanation: GKE Autopilot fully manages the node substrate — provisioning, upgrades, repairs and scaling — and prices per second by summed pod CPU/memory/ephemeral-storage requests, so idle node capacity is Google's problem, not yours. Cloud Run on GKE has been deprecated (superseded by Cloud Run and Cloud Run on Anthos), and even in its heyday it did not remove node-pool management from GKE. GKE Standard with node auto-upgrade still requires you to size and pay for node pools, so the 'pay only per pod' requirement is not met. There is no such thing as an 'Autopilot node pool' inside a Standard cluster — Autopilot is a cluster-wide mode, not a pool type.

questions.question: A company requires that only container images passing security scanning AND signed by the security team may deploy to GKE production. Which combination enforces this at admission time?
options: GKE admission webhooks that check Container Analysis scan results before allowing pods to start.
Cloud Build gating that refuses to push an image if any scan finding is above a threshold.
Binary Authorization policy requiring a KMS-signed security-team attestation on every image.
Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning configured to auto-block critical CVEs during push.
questions.explanation: Binary Authorization enforces its policy at pod admission time inside the GKE control plane: an image without a valid attestation from the required attestor is refused, no matter how it was pushed. A signed attestation is only created after the vulnerability scan passes, so the AND requirement is expressed as a single policy that GKE evaluates on every pod. GKE admission webhooks based only on scan results miss the signing requirement — anyone with kubectl and a passing scan could still deploy. Cloud Build gates and Artifact Registry auto-block only fire in the build/push path, so an image deployed directly to the cluster (or promoted from another registry) bypasses them entirely.

questions.question: A production e-commerce app on GKE went down when all its nodes lived in us-central1-a and that zone failed. Which configuration prevents future single-zone failures?
options: Create a regional GKE cluster spread across three zones and add pod anti-affinity so replicas land on different zones.
Enable GKE Autopilot mode and assume its scheduler will automatically distribute pods evenly across the region's zones.
Add Pod Disruption Budgets that keep no more than 50% of pods unavailable at once, so a zone loss cannot break majority.
Run one GKE cluster per zone with a global HTTP(S) load balancer in front of them for cross-zone request routing.
questions.explanation: A regional GKE cluster spreads its control plane across three zones and lets you place node pools across those same zones; combined with a pod anti-affinity rule keyed on topology.kubernetes.io/zone, replicas are pinned to different zones so any one zone can fail and the service stays up. Autopilot uses a regional control plane but does not by itself guarantee per-workload zone spread — it obeys whatever affinity/anti-affinity you set. PDBs limit voluntary disruptions (like node drains); an involuntary zone failure ignores them. Running one cluster per zone works but is far heavier than a single regional cluster with anti-affinity and duplicates all the operational overhead (upgrades, IAM, config).

questions.question: An SRE team has a 99.9% availability SLO for an API. They want alerts when the error budget is being consumed dangerously fast — not when random blips flap over the 5-minute error rate. Which alert should they configure?
options: A 30-day error-rate threshold that pages Pub/Sub when the rate exceeds the SLO objective.
A Dataflow pipeline that computes error-budget burn and pushes alerts through Cloud Tasks.
A burn-rate alert combining a short (1 h) window and a long (6 h) window on the SLO's SLI.
A Cloud Monitoring alert that fires when the error rate stays above 0.1% for 5 minutes.
questions.explanation: Multi-window burn-rate alerting is the SRE Workbook pattern for SLO-driven paging: the short window (about 1 hour) reacts quickly to a bad incident, the long window (about 6 hours) suppresses transient blips, and the burn multiplier tells you how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO period. Comparing the raw 30-day error rate to the SLO is too coarse: by the time it trips, the budget is already spent. A Dataflow-plus-Cloud-Tasks pipeline is an over-engineered reimplementation of what SLO burn-rate alerting already does natively. A fixed 0.1%/5-minute threshold ignores traffic volume entirely — the same 0.1% is trivial during peak hours and devastating during a low-traffic window.

questions.question: A genomics team runs 8–12 hour ML training jobs and wants to use cheap preemptible resources without losing training progress on preemption. Which approach is correct?
options: Have a startup script watch for the preemption notice and live-migrate the job to another Spot VM.
Run on Spot VMs with automatic restart, accepting that jobs restart from the beginning.
Schedule jobs on standard VMs during off-peak hours when preemptible availability is highest.
Add periodic checkpointing to Cloud Storage in the training code and run on Spot VMs.
questions.explanation: Periodic checkpointing to Cloud Storage plus Spot VMs is the standard cheap-training pattern: on preemption a replacement VM resumes from the last checkpoint, so worst-case loss is one checkpoint interval rather than the whole run. Live migration does not exist for Spot/preemptible VMs — the 30-second termination notice is exactly that, a notice — so any 'migrate to another Spot' scheme silently loses work. Accepting restarts from the beginning is the pattern that Spot VMs are cheap enough to make tempting, but for 8–12 hour runs it burns money on repeated work every preemption. Running on standard VMs off-peak forfeits the very Spot discount the question is trying to capture.

questions.question: A healthcare company must prevent BigQuery and Cloud Storage data exfiltration even if valid IAM credentials are stolen. Which control provides a security perimeter that blocks unauthorized API calls from outside?
options: A VPC Service Controls perimeter around BigQuery and Cloud Storage restricting requests to authorized networks.
Organization Policy constraints that prevent public access to BigQuery and Cloud Storage buckets.
IAM deny policies at the organization node that forbid external data-transfer operations.
Cloud DLP inspection inside a VPC perimeter that scans BigQuery exports and GCS downloads.
questions.explanation: VPC Service Controls draws a service-level boundary around GCP APIs: even a valid credential is refused unless the request originates from an authorized network (VPC, on-prem via Private Service Connect, or an ingress rule). That defeats the classic exfiltration pattern where an attacker uses a stolen key from their own laptop. Public-access Org Policy constraints only stop resources from being made anonymously readable — a stolen key is not anonymous. IAM deny policies apply to identities and specific method names; they do not distinguish 'from inside the perimeter' from 'from anywhere on the internet'. DLP inspection can classify data being moved but cannot by itself block calls from an outside credential — you would still need the perimeter.

questions.question: A containerized app on GKE reads from Cloud Storage and writes to BigQuery. Today, a service-account key file is mounted as a Kubernetes Secret. What is the recommended replacement?
options: Store the key in Secret Manager and inject it as an env var via a mutating webhook.
Have the pod call the GCE metadata server using the node's default service account.
Bind the Kubernetes service account to a Google service account with Workload Identity so no key file is needed.
Rotate the key every 24 hours via a Cloud Function that updates the Kubernetes Secret.
questions.explanation: Workload Identity is Google's recommended way to authenticate GKE workloads: a Kubernetes service account is bound to a Google service account, and pods using that KSA transparently receive short-lived tokens via the GKE metadata server — no long-lived key files anywhere. Storing the key in Secret Manager just moves the same long-lived credential to a different vault; it still ends up in the pod. Using the node's default service account gives every pod on the node identical, over-broad access — a textbook privilege-escalation risk. Aggressive 24-hour rotation shrinks the blast radius of a leaked key but keeps the leakable artifact and forces error-prone rotation plumbing when Workload Identity eliminates the key entirely.

questions.question: A retail site is under sustained attack: about 10 Gbps of L3/L4 flood traffic plus intermittent L7 SQL-injection attempts. Which Cloud Armor configuration protects against both?
options: Add per-IP throttling rules that cap any single client IP at 1,000 requests per second to blunt the DDoS traffic.
Configure custom Cloud Armor rules matching known-bad attacker IP ranges plus per-IP rate limits at the edge.
Enable Cloud Armor geo-restriction rules to block all traffic originating from countries where the attacks appear to originate.
Deploy Cloud Armor Managed Protection Plus with Adaptive Protection for L7 DDoS and preconfigured OWASP WAF rules.
questions.explanation: Managed Protection Plus fronts the Global HTTPS Load Balancer with Adaptive Protection — ML-driven L7 DDoS mitigation — and ships the preconfigured OWASP rules that stop SQLi, XSS and RCE, while Google's edge naturally absorbs the L3/L4 flood before it ever reaches your backends. A per-IP throttle does nothing against a distributed flood, because each of thousands of source IPs stays under the cap. Static IP blocklists lag real attacker rotation and miss the L7 layer altogether. Geo-restrictions punish legitimate users from those regions and are trivially bypassed by attackers using residential proxies elsewhere, so on their own they do not solve either problem.

questions.question: A company with strict data-sovereignty rules must own the encryption keys for BigQuery and Cloud Storage, and the keys must live in a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSM. Which solution fits?
options: Use Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK) generated on any FIPS HSM and passed to GCS on every request.
Rely on default Google-managed encryption combined with key-rotation audit logs.
Configure CMEK with keys stored in Cloud HSM (FIPS 140-2 Level 3) via Cloud KMS.
Use External Key Manager (EKM) with the key material hosted on an on-premises HSM.
questions.explanation: Cloud HSM keys are generated and used inside HSMs that are FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated and are exposed through Cloud KMS as CMEK, so both BigQuery datasets and Cloud Storage buckets can use them as their default encryption key while the customer retains lifecycle control (rotation, disable, destroy). CSEK requires you to supply the key on every call and is not supported by BigQuery at all. Google-managed encryption gives Google full key control, which is exactly the sovereignty requirement being rejected. External Key Manager satisfies the 'off Google' requirement but is a distinct architecture: the question specifies FIPS 140-2 Level 3 keys — the property Cloud HSM guarantees by construction — whereas EKM's FIPS level depends on the external HSM the customer runs.

questions.question: A security team wants to guarantee that no Compute Engine VM in the entire organization can be assigned an external IP. Which control scales best?
options: Set the constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess Organization Policy to Deny All at the organization node.
Deploy a Cloud Function on Cloud Asset Inventory notifications that strips external IPs from new VMs.
Configure VPC firewall rules in every project that drop all inbound/outbound traffic on external interfaces.
Create a custom IAM role removing compute.instances.setMachineType at the organization level.
questions.explanation: Organization Policy constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess is evaluated whenever a VM is created or updated; setting it to Deny All at the organization node cascades to every folder and project and refuses the request outright — no external IP can ever be attached. A remediation Cloud Function is best-effort: an external IP still exists between VM creation and the function's fix, and any bug in the function creates a permanent hole. VPC firewalls block traffic but leave the external IP assigned — the resource still exists and still costs money. Removing compute.instances.setMachineType has no relationship to external IPs; it just blocks machine-type changes.

questions.question: A large enterprise must log every Google employee access to customer data and require customer sign-off before Google support can access data. Which combination provides this?
options: Access Transparency (near-real-time Google-access logs) plus Access Approval (customer approves each request).
Context-Aware Access with identity conditions restricting all access to named service accounts.
VPC Service Controls plus restricted.googleapis.com to prevent Google infrastructure from reaching the project.
Cloud Audit Logs with data-access logs enabled, plus an internal ticket-based approval flow before Google support proceeds.
questions.explanation: Access Transparency emits near-real-time logs whenever Google staff access your content, including a justification code; Access Approval separately requires an explicit customer approval (via a signed request) before an eligible support access can proceed. Together they give the required visibility and the required veto. Context-Aware Access controls end-user access to your resources — it does nothing about Google-side access. VPC Service Controls fence customer identities, not Google support access, and restricted.googleapis.com only limits which Google APIs are reachable from a VPC. Data-access audit logs record customer-side access; they do not surface Google-employee actions, and an internal ticket cannot enforce a Google-side approval gate.

questions.question: A DevSecOps team requires images deployed to GKE production to carry TWO attestations: QA after test AND security after scan. Neither signature alone should be sufficient. Which Binary Authorization policy enforces this?
options: Deploy OPA Gatekeeper with a custom constraint template that validates both signatures at admission.
Add a Cloud Build step that checks for both signatures and refuses to push the image otherwise.
Create two Binary Authorization policies (one per attestor) and apply each to a separate namespace.
Configure one Binary Authorization policy with requireAttestationsBy listing both attestors.
questions.explanation: Binary Authorization's requireAttestationsBy accepts a list of attestors and requires ALL of them to have signed the image digest — a single policy expresses the QA-AND-security requirement and GKE enforces it at pod admission. OPA Gatekeeper can reimplement admission logic, but the question asks about Binary Authorization's native model, which already supports multi-attestor requirements without a custom constraint. A Cloud Build check only fires at build time and is bypassed by anyone who pushes or deploys another way. Splitting the policy across namespaces creates an OR relationship (whichever namespace a pod lands in only checks that one attestor), which is exactly what the requirement forbids.

questions.question: A team using CMEK for Cloud Storage needs the keys rotated every 90 days with the least operational effort. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Use Cloud Storage Batch Operations to re-encrypt every object with a new key every 90 days.
Set the Cloud KMS key's rotation period to 90 days so KMS creates a new primary version automatically.
Schedule a Cloud Scheduler job that calls the KMS API to create a new key version every 90 days.
Trigger a Cloud Function on a 90-day timer to bump the KMS primary version and update GCS.
questions.explanation: Cloud KMS supports built-in automatic rotation: set the key's rotation period to 90 days and KMS generates a new primary version on schedule, while older versions stay enabled for decryption. Cloud Storage's CMEK integration always encrypts new writes with the current primary, so nothing else is needed — the requirement is a two-field configuration change. Batch-re-encrypting every object achieves rotation but is enormously expensive and completely unnecessary because CMEK envelope encryption is per-object and does not require re-encrypting old data on rotation. Cloud Scheduler and Cloud Function timers reinvent the built-in feature and add code and monitoring that can silently fail.

questions.question: A company runs internal web apps that today are only protected by network firewalls. Employees need remote access without a VPN, and security requires zero-trust identity-aware access. What is the correct solution?
options: Configure site-to-site Cloud VPN tunnels from every employee's home network to the GCP VPC.
Use Private Google Access so authenticated Google accounts can reach private VPC services from the internet.
Enable Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) on the HTTPS load balancer fronting the apps.
Deploy Cloud Interconnect Partner links to each employee's ISP for private connectivity.
questions.explanation: Cloud IAP sits in front of an HTTPS load balancer and authenticates every request against Google Identity, then evaluates IAM and (optionally) Context-Aware Access conditions before proxying to the backend — a textbook zero-trust, per-request access model with no VPN. Site-to-site VPNs to residential networks are unmanageable at scale and grant network-level access rather than per-app identity-aware access. Private Google Access is for VMs inside a VPC reaching Google APIs privately — it is not an internet-facing authentication service. Cloud Interconnect is a physical connectivity option for offices and colos, not for individual employees.

questions.question: A microservices app scatters secrets across env vars, Kubernetes Secrets and config files. The security team wants centralized storage, rotation, and audit logging. What should you implement?
options: Deploy HashiCorp Vault on GKE as a sidecar per service for dynamic secret issuance.
Move everything into Secret Manager and read secrets at runtime via its client libraries.
Store secrets in Firestore with field-level CMEK encryption and restrict access with Firebase Security Rules.
Encrypt secrets with Cloud KMS and store the ciphertext blobs in Cloud Storage with per-object IAM.
questions.explanation: Secret Manager is the GCP-native secrets vault: it centralizes secret storage, supports versioning and rotation (natively or via Cloud Functions integrations), and every access shows up in Cloud Audit Logs — so applications fetch secrets at runtime via the client library rather than baking them into images or Kubernetes Secrets. HashiCorp Vault is powerful but is a self-managed system to operate and monitor; the question asks for a solution, and Secret Manager is the managed one. Firestore is a document database, not a secrets manager — Firebase Security Rules do not integrate with GCP IAM at the service-account level, and there is no version/rotation model out of the box. Storing KMS-encrypted blobs in GCS reproduces some of what Secret Manager provides but leaves rotation, versioning and audit plumbing as bespoke work.

questions.question: A CISO wants one place to see security findings, misconfigurations, vulnerabilities and compliance posture across every GCP project in the org. Which service provides this?
options: A Cloud Monitoring dashboard at the organization level aggregating metrics and logs from every project.
Security Command Center (SCC) Premium enabled at the organization level with continuous scanning.
Forseti Security Scanner running on a dedicated GKE cluster and scanning every project.
BigQuery log sinks from every project combined with custom SQL to detect security findings.
questions.explanation: Security Command Center Premium is Google's org-wide security posture and threat product: Security Health Analytics continuously scans for misconfigurations, Event Threat Detection and Container Threat Detection surface active threats, and findings are mapped to CIS, PCI, HIPAA and other frameworks — all in one console. Cloud Monitoring dashboards aggregate metrics, not security findings, and have no built-in threat intelligence. Forseti is the community predecessor to much of SCC's functionality and is no longer actively maintained by Google. BigQuery log sinks plus custom SQL is exactly the roll-your-own solution SCC exists to obviate — you would spend engineering time rebuilding scanners and mapping.

questions.question: An analytics company has unpredictable ad-hoc analyst queries and predictable overnight ETL batch jobs in BigQuery. How should they optimize cost?
options: Put every workload on on-demand pricing because it is always cheaper for mixed traffic.
Buy BigQuery Editions slot reservations for the ETL workload and leave analyst queries on on-demand.
Enable BI Engine reservations for all analyst queries to accelerate them with in-memory caching.
Buy flat-rate reserved slots covering every workload to make monthly spend predictable.
questions.explanation: The classic hybrid pattern is reservations for what is predictable and on-demand for what is not: reservations amortize a fixed baseline cost over the ETL workload where you know the slot draw, while analyst ad-hoc queries stay on on-demand pricing so you pay only for actual bytes scanned during their bursty use. Putting everything on on-demand is not 'always cheaper' — for a steady heavy workload, reservations are dramatically less expensive per slot-hour. BI Engine caches hot data for dashboard-style queries but is not a general cost tool for arbitrary ad-hoc queries. Reserving slots for the analyst workload also would leave slots unused whenever analysts are quiet, wasting the commitment.

questions.question: A retailer has 50 stable n2-standard-8 VMs running 24×7 and needs 200 additional VMs only during a 3-month holiday season. How should they minimize compute cost?
options: Buy 1-year Committed Use Discounts for the 50 stable VMs and run the 200 seasonal VMs on Spot.
Rely on Sustained Use Discounts alone by leaving all 250 VMs running continuously.
Buy 3-year Committed Use Discounts for all 250 VMs to maximize the discount rate.
Run all 250 VMs on Spot to capture the deepest per-hour discount.
questions.explanation: CUDs pay off when a workload is predictable and always on, which fits the 50 stable VMs precisely; Spot VMs are 60–90% cheaper than on-demand and are appropriate for transient, interruptible workloads like the holiday burst. SUDs alone are automatic but shallower than CUDs and give you no discount for the seasonal VMs, which don't run enough of the year to benefit either way. Buying CUDs for the seasonal 200 wastes the commitment for the nine off-months. Running the stable catalog service on Spot risks unpredictable preemption on a workload that is not designed for it and forfeits the CUD savings.

questions.question: A media streaming company serves 4K video globally and needs edge caching, DDoS protection and routing to the nearest healthy origin. Which architecture provides all three natively?
options: Regional Cloud Storage buckets fronted by Cloudflare CDN with Cloud DNS latency routing.
Regional HTTPS load balancers in each market plus Security Command Center for DDoS alerting.
Cloud Interconnect links to external DDoS scrubbing providers plus a third-party CDN.
A Global External HTTPS Load Balancer with Cloud CDN enabled and Cloud Armor Adaptive Protection.
questions.explanation: The GCP-native three-tier answer is a Global HTTPS Load Balancer for anycast routing to the closest healthy origin, Cloud CDN for edge caching of video segments, and Cloud Armor Adaptive Protection for L3/L4 and L7 DDoS mitigation at Google's edge — all one integrated stack. Third-party CDNs and external scrubbing add integration surface and split responsibility. Regional load balancers plus latency DNS give you neither anycast failover nor Google-edge DDoS absorption. Security Command Center surfaces findings; it is not an in-line DDoS mitigation, so relying on it for protection leaves your origin exposed.

questions.question: A backend Python service is spiking CPU in production. You need to see which functions are burning the most CPU without adding meaningful overhead. Which tool fits?
options: Use Cloud Debugger to capture production snapshots at the suspected hotspots.
Enable Cloud Profiler, which samples production continuously at under 1% overhead.
Instrument Cloud Trace on every function call and analyse the longest spans.
Add Python's cProfile in production and export the profiles to Cloud Storage nightly.
questions.explanation: Cloud Profiler is a statistical sampling profiler designed to run continuously in production: it samples call stacks, tags them by CPU and memory, and renders flame graphs — all at under 1% CPU overhead, which is the constraint the question makes explicit. Cloud Debugger (now retired) captured state at breakpoints and never produced aggregate CPU-time views. Cloud Trace measures request-level latency across services, not per-function CPU time — a slow span could be waiting on I/O with no CPU at all. cProfile is deterministic and has such high overhead that Python's own documentation warns against running it in production.

questions.question: A GKE cluster has pods with resource requests set far higher than actual usage, wasting node capacity. You want to automatically right-size the requests based on real usage. Which component fits?
options: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with custom metrics that scales replicas on observed usage.
Cluster Autoscaler configured with a bin-packing strategy so nodes fill more tightly.
GKE Node Auto Provisioning that spawns node pools sized for the current workload.
Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode, which continuously updates CPU/memory requests.
questions.explanation: The Vertical Pod Autoscaler observes historical usage and, in Auto mode, evicts pods and restarts them with recomputed requests and limits — directly attacking the over-requested-CPU/memory problem in the question. HPA scales the number of replicas; it does not resize any individual pod's requests. Cluster Autoscaler decides how many nodes to run based on unscheduled pods; it does not shrink pod requests, so an over-requested pod keeps its wasted headroom. Node Auto Provisioning picks node shapes to match pod requests, so it will happily provision oversized nodes for the current oversized requests — it treats the requests as ground truth.

questions.question: A company wants events from Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, BigQuery jobs and Cloud Audit Logs to reach Cloud Run and Cloud Functions through a unified, standards-based event bus. Which service provides this?
options: Separate Pub/Sub topics per event source with push subscriptions targeting each service.
A Cloud Scheduler + Pub/Sub loop that polls each service on a fixed cadence.
A Cloud Functions dispatcher that subscribes to all sources and re-emits events to each target.
Eventarc, which routes events from GCP sources to Cloud Run, Cloud Functions and GKE in CloudEvents format.
questions.explanation: Eventarc is Google's managed event router: it consumes events from Cloud Audit Logs (which covers most GCP services), Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub and third-party sources, and delivers them in the CNCF CloudEvents format to Cloud Run, Cloud Functions and GKE workflows. Building this yourself out of per-source Pub/Sub topics recreates the schema-normalization and routing plumbing Eventarc already provides. Cloud Scheduler is a cron service, not an event bus, and polling is the anti-pattern event-driven architectures exist to remove. A hand-rolled Cloud Functions dispatcher is exactly the fragile fan-out layer that led Google to build Eventarc.

questions.question: A Django app on Cloud SQL PostgreSQL has read bottlenecks with a 90/10 read/write ratio. Which approach scales reads with the least operational effort?
options: Introduce Memorystore (Redis) in front of Cloud SQL and cache frequent SELECT results.
Deploy PgBouncer on Cloud Run for connection pooling to relieve connection pressure.
Migrate to Cloud Spanner, which scales reads and writes horizontally.
Add Cloud SQL read replicas and route SELECT traffic to them, keeping writes on the primary.
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL read replicas are a few clicks or API calls away, need no schema change, and let the Django database router send SELECT queries to the replica pool while writes stay on the primary — the cheapest change that hits the read bottleneck head-on. Memorystore adds a genuine performance boost but forces cache-invalidation logic into the application, which is significant new complexity, not less. PgBouncer helps when connections are the constraint but does not address per-query read throughput. Migrating a live Django app to Spanner is a major porting effort (dialect differences, JOIN and index behavior, application changes) — far from 'least operational effort'.

questions.question: A BI team's Looker dashboards backed by BigQuery show 10–20 second query latency. Dashboards repeatedly hit the same slice of data. Which optimization brings latency into the sub-second range?
options: Route dashboard queries through BigQuery Omni to a nearer regional compute resource.
Convert BigQuery tables to column-store format and cluster them on every dashboard filter.
Create BigQuery materialized views for each dashboard query with automatic refresh.
Enable BigQuery BI Engine with a capacity reservation so hot data is served from memory.
questions.explanation: BI Engine keeps frequently accessed data resident in memory and serves queries against it in milliseconds; because it is integrated with the BigQuery API, Looker and Looker Studio benefit transparently without query rewrites — precisely the sub-second target the scenario names. BigQuery Omni exists to query data that lives in AWS or Azure, not to reduce latency on data already in BigQuery. BigQuery tables are already columnar, so 'converting' them is a no-op, and adding clustering on every dashboard filter is not always possible (you can cluster on at most four columns) and rarely delivers sub-second response by itself. Materialized views help specific aggregate queries but require query patterns to line up with the view definition — BI Engine is transparent and covers repeated dashboard slices more broadly.

questions.question: A microservices app has intermittent high latency on checkout requests that traverse eight services. The team cannot reproduce it locally. Which tool identifies exactly which service and operation is the bottleneck?
options: Enable Cloud Trace with sampling on all services and inspect the waterfall for the slow requests.
Deploy Prometheus and Jaeger sidecars in GKE to capture distributed traces independently.
Build Cloud Monitoring dashboards showing p95 latency per service to spot the slowest.
Correlate error logs across the eight services via a shared trace_id in Cloud Logging.
questions.explanation: Cloud Trace's distributed-tracing waterfall stitches spans from every service under a shared trace ID and shows exactly how much time each hop and each operation consumed — the exact insight the scenario asks for. Prometheus + Jaeger can produce the same view but is a self-managed stack when Google already provides the managed one; the question asks for the tool, not for how to reimplement it. Aggregate p95 dashboards flag a slow service but never explain which downstream call within it caused a given slow request. Correlating error logs is powerful once you know what to look for, but log lines carry no timing spans, so they cannot themselves point to the bottleneck operation.

questions.question: A large enterprise wants a BI platform where analysts define reusable business metrics ('Monthly Active Users', 'Revenue per Region') in a semantic layer shared by every dashboard. Which GCP tool supports this pattern?
options: Data Catalog with business-glossary entries linked to BigQuery columns.
Looker Studio with per-dashboard calculated fields to standardize metric definitions.
BigQuery BI Engine plus authorized views that encapsulate business logic for dashboards.
Looker (LookML), which defines a centralized semantic data model that every explore and dashboard consumes.
questions.explanation: Looker's LookML is a semantic layer: 'Monthly Active Users' is defined once in a model, and every explore, dashboard and API query uses that definition — solving the classic 'each dashboard computes MAU slightly differently' problem the question describes. Data Catalog stores metadata about tables and columns; it does not power dashboard calculations. Looker Studio calculated fields live inside each report, so there is no shared source of truth. Authorized views can encapsulate SQL logic but expose it as views to consume; they are not a metric-modeling layer with dimensions, measures and joins the way LookML is.

questions.question: A payment app on GKE must comply with PCI DSS. Cardholder-data-environment (CDE) pods must only talk to explicitly authorized services and must not reach other pods in the cluster. What should you configure?
options: A default-deny NetworkPolicy on the CDE namespace with explicit allow rules for authorized pods and ports.
Istio service mesh with mTLS to encrypt all pod-to-pod traffic in the cluster.
Cloud Armor policies to restrict inter-pod traffic inside the GKE cluster.
Node taints and tolerations so CDE pods only run on dedicated nodes.
questions.explanation: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is enforced at L3/L4 by GKE's network plugin: applying a default-deny ingress-and-egress policy to the CDE namespace, then adding narrowly scoped allow rules for the specific pods and ports required, gives you the segmentation PCI DSS demands. Istio mTLS encrypts and authenticates the traffic but does not, by itself, prevent one pod from talking to another. Cloud Armor is an edge-layer WAF/DDoS product and does not operate on pod-to-pod traffic. Node taints and tolerations control scheduling — CDE pods on dedicated nodes still have full network reachability to any other pod in the cluster unless you add a NetworkPolicy anyway.

questions.question: An e-commerce site runs in three regions. SREs want to be alerted when the site is unreachable from multiple geographic locations at once, but not on single-region blips that resolve in under two minutes. What configuration achieves this?
options: One uptime check probed from multiple global locations, plus a multi-condition alert that fires only when several probe locations fail together for a sustained window.
Cloud Trace watching request failure rates with an alert that pages when server-side errors exceed 5% inside any single region for one minute.
Deploy synthetic Cloud Functions in each region that write custom availability metrics into Cloud Monitoring and alert whenever any function errors.
Three independent per-region uptime-check alerts, each firing after five minutes of failure in that region regardless of the other regions.
questions.explanation: A single uptime check with probes in multiple global locations plus a multi-condition alert lets you require simultaneous multi-location failure for a chosen minimum duration — exactly matching 'multiple regions, not a two-minute blip'. Cloud Trace measures user request latency and errors on already-served traffic; it cannot probe from outside the service, so it cannot tell you the site is unreachable. Custom synthetic Cloud Functions can work, but they reimplement uptime checks by hand for no benefit. Three independent per-region alerts each fire on their own — you would still get paged for a single-region blip, which is the noise the requirement is written to avoid.

questions.question: A multi-stage pipeline promotes builds dev → staging → production. Operations must manually approve every production deployment, and prod must use the exact artifact that passed staging. Which GCP service enforces this natively?
options: Deploy ArgoCD on GKE with manual sync policies configured against the production environment target.
Build one Cloud Build pipeline per environment with a manual-approval step wired between the staging and production pipelines.
Use a custom Cloud Functions webhook that blocks each deployment until an IAM policy condition is externally satisfied.
Cloud Deploy with a delivery pipeline where the production target requires approval, so the same release progresses through all stages.
questions.explanation: Cloud Deploy is the managed continuous-delivery service on GCP: a release is a specific container-image + manifest bundle that flows through pipeline targets (dev → staging → prod), and setting requireApproval on the production target pauses the promotion until an authorized human clicks approve. Same release, same artifact, native audit trail. ArgoCD works but is a third-party tool the question is stepping away from. Cloud Build can wait for approval but is a CI tool; using it as a deployment orchestrator loses the release/rollout state model that Cloud Deploy provides. A custom Cloud Function webhook is exactly the ad hoc glue Cloud Deploy exists to replace.

questions.question: A team pushes images to Artifact Registry. They want to guarantee that ONLY images from their own Artifact Registry can be deployed to GKE — no Docker Hub, no Quay, no external registries. How should they enforce this?
options: Create an Organization Policy that restricts allowed container registries to Artifact Registry only.
Enable Container Analysis on Artifact Registry so unscanned images are refused for deployment.
Deploy GKE private nodes and block egress to the IP ranges of external container registries.
Configure a Binary Authorization policy with an allowlist of Artifact Registry image paths and a deny-all default.
questions.explanation: Binary Authorization is the admission-time control: an allowlist of image paths (for example projects/PROJECT/locations/*/repositories/*) combined with a default-deny policy means GKE refuses to run any image whose registry path is not in the allowlist, no matter how it was staged. There is no Organization Policy constraint that limits GKE to a specific registry — that is exactly what Binary Authorization exists to express. Container Analysis is a scanning integration, not a source-of-image control; an unsigned image can still be deployed if the admission policy does not require the attestation. Blocking egress to external registry IPs is a moving-target denylist that misses new registries and mirrors — and does not prevent someone sideloading an image via a private mirror.

questions.question: A team wants a CI pipeline that builds a Docker image, runs unit tests, scans for vulnerabilities, and pushes a signed image to Artifact Registry — triggered on every Git commit. What is the GCP-native implementation?
options: Run a Jenkins master on Compute Engine and orchestrate the pipeline with GCP-specific plugins.
Cloud Composer DAGs on a commit webhook that orchestrate Docker build/test/push steps.
A cloudbuild.yaml with sequential build/test/scan/sign steps and a Cloud Build trigger on repository push.
Cloud Functions triggered by Cloud Source Repositories push events running each CI stage.
questions.explanation: Cloud Build is the native GCP CI service: cloudbuild.yaml defines ordered steps (docker build, tests, gcloud artifacts docker images scan, attestation signing), and a Cloud Build trigger fires on every push. It is integrated with Artifact Registry, Container Analysis and Binary Authorization end-to-end. Jenkins works but is self-managed and third-party — the opposite of what 'GCP-native' asks for. Cloud Composer is an Airflow-based workflow orchestrator built for data pipelines, not CI. Cloud Functions can run individual stages, but stitching together a real CI pipeline out of Functions ends up recreating what Cloud Build already provides.

questions.question: A platform team manages GCP policies and Kubernetes configurations across 15 GKE clusters. They want a single Git repository as the source of truth, automatically applied to every cluster. Which capability enables that?
options: Cloud Deployment Manager applying Kubernetes YAML from a Git repo to every cluster.
Config Sync (part of Anthos Config Management), which continuously reconciles cluster state from a Git repository.
Helm with a central chart repository and ArgoCD ApplicationSets syncing across clusters.
Cloud Build triggers running kubectl apply against all 15 clusters on every Git change.
questions.explanation: Config Sync installs an in-cluster agent that continuously watches a Git repository and reconciles the cluster to match it, with support for root sync plus per-namespace RepoSyncs — the GCP-native, fleet-wide GitOps model. Cloud Deployment Manager does not manage cross-cluster Kubernetes GitOps and is in maintenance mode. Helm plus ArgoCD ApplicationSets can achieve the same shape but is a third-party stack when the question asks for a native capability. Cloud Build triggers running kubectl apply are imperative CI operations with no drift reconciliation — if someone mutates a cluster between commits, that drift persists until the next Git change.

questions.question: A GKE Deployment was rolled to a new image that immediately started crashing. It has been failing for five minutes and must be rolled back to the last working version as fast as possible. What is the fastest recovery?
options: Edit the manifest in Git to revert the image tag and wait for CI/CD to redeploy.
kubectl delete the Deployment, then kubectl apply the previous manifest.
kubectl edit the Deployment image tag directly and save.
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> to restore the previous ReplicaSet immediately.
questions.explanation: Kubernetes keeps ReplicaSet history for every Deployment, and 'kubectl rollout undo' instantly switches back to the previous ReplicaSet — no Git commit, no CI wait, no downtime beyond the rolling swap. Reverting in Git and waiting for CI is correct in principle but adds pipeline latency exactly when you least want it. Deleting the Deployment causes a hard outage window during the gap between delete and re-apply. Manually kubectl edit-ing the image works, but you have to know the exact previous tag and get the syntax right under pressure — rollout undo does the same thing with one command and no chance of typos.

questions.question: A developer needs to run a video-transcoding job that requires 32 GB of RAM and takes up to 75 minutes, triggered by Pub/Sub when new video files land in Cloud Storage. Which compute option supports both requirements?
options: App Engine Flexible Environment with a custom runtime sized for 32 GB memory.
Cloud Run jobs, which support up to 32 GB memory and per-job execution times measured in hours.
Cloud Run services with min-instances=1 to guarantee the container stays warm for the transcoding call.
Cloud Functions 2nd gen, which supports 32 GB RAM and one-hour timeouts on all runtimes.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run jobs (as opposed to Cloud Run services) are designed for finite, long-running batch work: up to 32 GB memory and execution times that comfortably cover a 75-minute transcoding pass; a Pub/Sub push subscription can trigger the job via Eventarc when files arrive. App Engine Flexible can hit 32 GB but is a heavier deployment target and is being wound down by Google. Cloud Run services are gated by a per-request timeout that is well under 75 minutes, so a 75-minute request would be killed mid-flight. Cloud Functions 2nd gen supports 32 GB, but its per-request timeout for HTTP-triggered functions still tops out below 75 minutes — the wrong runtime for a job of this length.

questions.question: An SRE team is writing SLOs for a payment API. Product agreed that 99.95% of valid payment requests over a 30-day rolling window should succeed with HTTP 2xx. How should the SLI be expressed?
options: SLI = 1 − error_rate on all HTTP responses, including client 4xx; SLO = SLI ≥ 99.95% over 30 days.
SLI = count(HTTP 2xx responses) / count(valid payment requests); SLO = SLI ≥ 99.95% over the 30-day window.
SLI = count(requests under 200 ms) / count(total requests); SLO = SLI ≥ 99.95% to combine availability and latency.
SLI = uptime_minutes / total_minutes_in_30_days; SLO = SLI ≥ 99.95% as time-based availability.
questions.explanation: The SLI must reflect the user-facing behaviour the SLO promises — successful payments — so it is a ratio of successful (HTTP 2xx) responses to valid payment requests. Client 4xx errors are usually excluded because they represent bad client input, not service failure; conflating them with server errors punishes the service for user mistakes. A single-metric SLI cannot mix availability and latency without hiding one behind the other; latency belongs to its own separate SLO. Time-based availability (uptime minutes) is a weaker proxy than request-based availability — a service can be 'up' the whole minute while returning errors for many of the requests inside it.

questions.question: An SRE team wants to be paged within an hour if the 30-day error budget for a 99.9% SLO is being consumed fast enough to exhaust in under three days. Which alert should they configure?
options: A multi-window burn-rate alert combining a short (1 h) window and a long (6 h) window with a 10× burn threshold.
A Dataflow job that computes real-time burn rate and publishes alerts through Pub/Sub.
A fixed threshold that fires when the 30-day cumulative error budget drops below 50%.
A Cloud Monitoring alert that fires when the past-5-minute error rate exceeds 0.1%.
questions.explanation: The SRE Workbook multi-window burn-rate alert is exactly this shape: a short window (about 1 hour) catches the incident quickly, a long window (about 6 hours) suppresses transient spikes, and a 10× burn rate on a 99.9% SLO would consume the monthly budget in 72 hours — the alerting boundary in the question. Reimplementing burn-rate computation on Dataflow is an operational tax with no benefit — Cloud Monitoring SLOs already expose burn-rate signals. A cumulative-budget threshold trips much later than a burn-rate signal — by 50% consumption on day 10 you have already burned through fast; the question wants an early signal. A raw 0.1%-in-5-minutes rule is traffic-agnostic and generates noise during low-traffic periods.

questions.question: A company running Cloud SQL for MySQL has an RPO of 4 hours and an RTO of 2 hours. A DBA accidentally dropped a critical table. Which Cloud SQL configuration lets them recover within those objectives?
options: Automated backups every hour and restore the most recent full backup.
Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR) with binary logging: clone the instance to a timestamp just before the drop.
A read replica that is promoted as a DR target, then rolled forward from binary-log backups.
A Cloud SQL HA instance whose standby automatically fails over within minutes.
questions.explanation: PITR uses binary transaction logs to reconstruct the database to any second within the retention window: clone the instance to the moment just before the accidental DROP, then swing traffic — comfortably under a 2-hour RTO, and with hourly resolution well inside the 4-hour RPO. Restoring only from automated backups is coarser than PITR and might lose everything between the last backup and the drop. Promoting a read replica does not help: replication faithfully forwarded the DROP statement, so the replica is missing the table too. HA fails over between replicas that share the same data — the dropped table is dropped on both sides.

questions.question: An SRE team wants to prove that Cloud SQL HA actually fails over correctly during zone outages. They want to test in production during a low-traffic window. What is the chaos-engineering approach?
options: Trigger a Cloud SQL HA failover during low-traffic hours while monitoring SLIs and application behaviour.
Wait for a real zone outage and use the post-incident review to identify failover gaps.
Test only in a staging environment that mirrors production traffic.
Run Cloud SQL's built-in test failover during a maintenance window without watching SLIs.
questions.explanation: Chaos engineering is proactive fault injection under controlled conditions with instrumentation in place: firing a Cloud SQL HA failover during low-traffic hours while watching connection pools, latency, error rates and reconnection behaviour exposes the real RTO and reveals subtle issues (DNS TTL, driver reconnect, connection-pool warm-up) that staging cannot reproduce. Waiting for a real outage means you learn everything the hard way, exactly what chaos engineering aims to avoid. Staging alone rarely mirrors production traffic mix, connection counts or client SDK versions accurately enough. Firing the test failover without monitoring SLIs tells you the API succeeded but leaves the actual user-facing impact unmeasured.

questions.question: Cloud Logging costs are spiking because a verbose web server is emitting a torrent of DEBUG lines. Developers still want to see them but do not need them retained in Cloud Logging. Which change reduces ingestion cost?
options: Extend the _Default bucket retention period to 30 days to spread ingestion cost.
Add a Cloud Logging exclusion filter targeting that log name and severity=DEBUG so those entries are never ingested.
Route DEBUG logs through a log sink that excludes them from _Default but writes them to BigQuery.
Disable logging entirely for the project and stream logs to a Cloud Storage bucket via a sink.
questions.explanation: Cloud Logging exclusion filters drop matching entries at the ingestion boundary — you are not billed for what is never ingested — which is the direct answer to a Cloud Logging bill dominated by DEBUG traffic. Extending retention makes things worse because ingestion is billed independently of storage duration. A log sink still ingests the log entry first (so ingestion cost stays) and then adds BigQuery storage and streaming costs on top. Disabling logging entirely is a blunt instrument — you lose the ERROR and WARNING lines the developers need, and streaming to Cloud Storage still requires ingestion.

questions.question: A company must ensure Pub/Sub message data is stored only inside EU data centres to meet GDPR. Which Pub/Sub feature enforces this?
options: Create the topic in a europe-west region with message retention enabled to automatically restrict data to EU data centres.
Enable CMEK on the topic with a Cloud KMS key in an EU region.
Configure a message-storage policy on the topic that restricts allowed persistence regions to EU regions.
Use VPC Service Controls to restrict Pub/Sub access to EU IP ranges.
questions.explanation: Pub/Sub is a global service by default: setting a message-storage policy on the topic explicitly restricts the set of regions where message data may be persisted at rest, so choosing only EU regions (europe-west1, europe-west4, europe-north1, …) is the direct way to enforce EU-only storage. Selecting a europe-west 'region' when creating a topic is a UX affordance; without a message-storage policy the underlying storage can still fall back to other regions. CMEK controls encryption keys, not data residency — a KMS key in the EU does not stop the ciphertext from being replicated elsewhere. VPC Service Controls is a request-boundary control; it restricts who can call the API, not where message data is stored on disk.

questions.question: A 99.9% monthly availability SLO service had 25 minutes of downtime in a 30-day window (43,200 total minutes). A new deployment carries a 15-minute downtime risk. What is the true error-budget status?
options: Error budget = 43.2 min; 25 min consumed leaves 18.2 min; the 15-min-risk deployment would eat 82% of what's left and is risky.
Error budget = 43.2 min; 25 min consumed = 58% remaining; safe to proceed since more than 50% remains.
Error budget = 43.2 min; 25 min consumed = 42% remaining; budget is insufficient for a 15-minute deployment.
Error budget = 4.32 min; 25 minutes consumed means the SLO is already breached; do not proceed.
questions.explanation: The monthly error budget is (1 − 0.999) × 43,200 = 43.2 minutes; after 25 minutes consumed you are left with 18.2 minutes (about 42%). A deployment carrying a 15-minute risk would consume 15/18.2 ≈ 82% of that remainder and leave essentially no runway for the rest of the month — technically feasible but a very poor risk/reward trade. The 42% figure alone is correct but omits the specific-risk analysis the question asks for. Calling 58% remaining is a wrong subtraction. The 4.32-minute budget corresponds to a 99.99% SLO, not 99.9%.

questions.question: A team launches a new microservice that processes credit-card payments. The SRE team requires a Production Readiness Review (PRR). Which aspects must the PRR validate before launch?
options: GKE Autopilot resource requests, Cloud Monitoring dashboard completeness and Cloud SQL PITR enabled.
Code-review completion, unit-test coverage above 80% and a successful staging deployment.
Defined SLIs/SLOs with error budgets, burn-rate alerting, runbooks, capacity plan, rollback plan and security review.
Cloud Armor WAF configuration, Binary Authorization attestations and CMEK key-rotation schedule.
questions.explanation: A PRR audits the whole reliability and operability posture: SLIs/SLOs with error budgets in place, burn-rate alerting that fires before users are impacted, runbooks for expected failure modes, capacity plan for peak and 2× peak, a tested rollback path, and a completed security/threat review. Individual controls like GKE requests, dashboards or CMEK rotation are inputs — necessary but far from a complete PRR. Code review and staging deployments are engineering hygiene, not reliability posture. WAF and Binary Authorization matter for a payments service, but a PRR is broader than any single security control.

questions.question: Which TWO Google Cloud load balancers can serve as a global anycast frontend with a single external IP that routes to the closest healthy backend?
options: External HTTP(S) Load Balancer (Global).
External TCP/UDP Network Load Balancer (regional Maglev).
External SSL Proxy Load Balancer (Global).
Internal Regional TCP/UDP Load Balancer.
questions.explanation: The global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer and the External SSL Proxy Load Balancer both use one anycast VIP announced from every Google edge and route to the closest healthy backend over Google's private backbone. The Network Load Balancer is regional (backed by Maglev) and does not present a global anycast frontend. Internal Load Balancers are regional by definition and not reachable from the internet, so they cannot act as a global external frontend.
